interest: This document provides a fascinating glimpse into early interwar Japanese commercial and geopolitical expansion in French Morocco during the 1930s. It highlights how Japanese commercial agents were perceived by American observers as actively seeking to supplant American trade while deliberately cultivating anti-American sentiment among native and mixed-race populations. Furthermore, it illustrates the intelligence networks of U.S. diplomats, who gathered sensitive political observations through high-level indigenous contacts such as Prince Mehdi El Glaoui while he was undergoing military training in France.
overview: This file consists of a single U.S. Department of State document file cross-reference sheet (decimal file 894.20281/1), dated September 28, 1933, indexing despatch No. W.D. 1312 from Claude I. Dawson in France, originally filed under 681.9417/1. The document records confidential intelligence relayed by Prince Mehdi El Glaoui, son of the Pasha of Marrakech, while completing his military studies in France. The report details active efforts by Japanese commercial agents in Morocco to displace American trade in favor of Japanese commerce and to foster anti-American sentiment among the local Moroccan population.

subfiles.summary: This State Department cross-reference sheet references despatch No. W.D. 1312 dated September 28, 1933, sent from France by Claude I. Dawson and classified under 681.9417/1. It summarizes private intelligence received from Prince Mehdi El Glaoui, son of the Pasha of Morocco, who was then pursuing military training in France. Prince Mehdi reported that Japanese commercial agents in Morocco were aggressively attempting to supplant American commerce with Japanese trade and were actively inciting anti-American sentiment among native populations.
